paper_context.research_question: Can a unified macro–micro discourse representation (integrating pragmatic macro schematic functions and micro-level rhetorical/nuclearity relations) be defined and annotated for Chinese news, and is such a Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank suitable for supporting automatic recognition of discourse relations and primary-secondary (primary/nucleus) relations?
main_claims: A macro-micro unified discourse representation schema that couples micro (rhetorical/logical) structure with macro (schematic/pragmatic) structure and a primary-secondary relation defined at both levels is appropriate for discourse structure analysis.

The authors provide a Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB) of 97 Xinhua news articles annotated according to this schema (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations), enabling joint study of macro schematic functions and micro rhetorical relations.

Preliminary supervised experiments on discourse-relation recognition and primary-secondary relation recognition using features derived from the corpus yield reasonable performance (e.g., primary-secondary F-scores reported per class), supporting the usefulness of the schema and resource.
There is observable dependency between discourse relation types and primary-secondary assignments (e.g., joint relations are multi-primary; elaboration tends to have the nucleus in the former unit).
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Annotation scheme clarity and theoretical grounding (how well macro pragmatic functions and micro rhetorical relations are defined and motivated).
Annotation quality and reliability (inter-annotator agreement, kappa on structural and relation labels, coverage of annotation guidelines).
Corpus size, representativeness and documentation (97 news articles: adequacy for downstream tasks, genre balance, availability of full texts and annotation formats).
Empirical utility: baseline model performance for discourse relation recognition and primary-secondary classification, including handling of class imbalance and feature design.
Novelty relative to existing discourse resources (what is new compared to RST-DT, PDTB, CDT and prior Chinese resources) and potential to enable new tasks.
Reproducibility: availability of data, annotation guidelines, and code to replicate experiments.
Granularity and consistency of the macro–micro integration (e.g., mapping between paragraph-level macro labels and EDU-level micro labels).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a unified macro–micro discourse representation for Chinese news that couples paragraph-level pragmatic schematic functions with EDU-level micro rhetorical relations and defines a primary-secondary (P-S / S-P / MP) relation at both levels. The authors produce MCDTB (97 Xinhua articles) annotated per this schema, report corpus statistics (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations) and annotator-consistency checks (Table 4 referenced), and run preliminary supervised experiments (maximum-entropy, hand-crafted features, 10-fold CV, resampling) for primary-secondary and discourse relation recognition. The central argumentative chain is: (1) existing micro theories (e.g., CDT/RST) lack macro pragmatic modeling; (2) a unified schema better captures discourse intention by adding schematic functions and global primary-secondary judgments; (3) the annotated MCDTB demonstrates feasibility; (4) classifier results and distributional statistics show dependency patterns and support the schema's usefulness. The manuscript is coherent in narrative but several inferential steps (reliability of macro labels, statistical strength of dependency claims, reproducibility of experiments) are under-supported by explicit data or methodology detail, weakening the force of the conclusions beyond the 'preliminary' scope.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Micro-level discourse theories (RST/CDT) capture local rhetorical relations and nuclearity but focus on logical semantics -> Evidence: RST discussion (Intro, 2.1) and CDT citation (Li et al., 2014).

P2: Macro-level theories (Van Dijk, schematic structures) capture global pragmatics; current work neglects combining micro and macro pragmatic functions -> Evidence: Van Dijk citations and Figure 3 schematic structure discussion.

Step A (Motivation): Because micro nuclearity is local and macro structure is pragmatic, a unified macro–micro schema that defines primary-secondary at both levels should better represent discourse intention -> Supported by conceptual argument in Section 1 and Section 3.

Step B (Representation): Define a hierarchical tree (title, chapter, paragraph, microstructure, EDU) where paragraphs are macro-layer leaf nodes and relations are non-leaf nodes; primary units are arrow targets -> Evidence: Section 3, Figures 4–7, Table 3.

Step C (Operationalization): Annotate 97 Xinhua articles following top-down + bottom-up strategy; apply local/global principles for P-S judgments -> Evidence: Section 4.1–4.2, annotation strategy description.
Step D (Quality assurance): Measure annotator consistency (agreement, kappa) on 20 docs to demonstrate reliability -> Evidence: Section 4.3 references Table 4 (numbers not shown in excerpt).

Step E (Descriptive patterns): Corpus statistics (Table 5) and relation-to-primary distribution (Table 6) show strong dependence between relation type and primary-secondary pattern (e.g., all Joint -> MP; all Elaboration -> P-S) -> Evidence: Table 5–6, Section 4.4 commentary.

Step F (Empirical validation): Train maximum entropy classifiers with hand-crafted features under 10-fold CV and resampling to obtain baseline performance for primary-secondary and relation recognition; reported F-scores support feasibility -> Evidence: Section 5, Tables 7–9.

Conclusion (Claim): The combined resource and schema are appropriate and useful for discourse structure analysis in Chinese news, supported by annotation and preliminary experiments -> Supported by Steps A–F but qualified as 'preliminary'.

Assumption A1 in shared analysis flags the risk if paragraphs are not coherent macro units.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report analysis of paragraph homogeneity: sample paragraphs, annotate or measure whether multiple schematic functions occur within single paragraphs; consider experiments that re-segment paragraphs into EDUs for comparison and report impact on macro annotations and classifier performance.

uncertainty_flags: Public availability of MCDTB and annotation guidelines is not confirmed; reproducibility depends on release.

alternative_interpretations: Observed deterministic patterns (e.g., Joint -> MP) reflect annotation conventions by design (e.g., definition of 'Joint' implies multi-primary) rather than empirical discovery—thus the dependency could be tautological.

High performance on some primary-secondary classes may result from class-size effects, resampling, or simple positional heuristics (e.g., beginning-of-article units are often primary) rather than deep semantic modeling.

The paragraph-as-leaf choice may obscure useful micro–macro interactions: in cases where paragraphs contain mixed functions, macro labels reflect the dominant function but lose nuance, biasing model learning.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The lack of a close analog (a Chinese resource that jointly annotates paragraph-level pragmatics with micro rhetorical relations and unified primary-secondary arrows) is a potential innovation signal, but novelty alone does not establish annotation reliability or downstream utility; empirical robustness and public release are required to convert novelty into impact.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the annotation guidelines are made exhaustive with clear conversion rules between micro relations and macro schematic functions and annotator training is thorough, inter-annotator agreement will improve and the resource will be reliable.
If the MCDTB is released publicly with formats and scripts, other researchers can reproduce experiments and extend corpus size (e.g., other news sources), enabling stronger empirical validation.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a unified macro–micro discourse representation for Chinese news that couples paragraph-level schematic/pragmatic functions with EDU-level rhetorical relations and a primary-secondary (P-S/S-P/MP) relation defined at both scales. Guided by this schema the authors annotated 97 Xinhua articles (MCDTB) building on CTB/CDT conventions (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations). They report annotation quality checks on 20 documents (agreement/Kappa referenced but numbers not present in the excerpt) and present descriptive statistics (Table 5, Table 6) showing strong dependence between relation types and primary-secondary assignments (e.g., all Joint relations are MP; all Elaboration relations are P-S). Preliminary supervised experiments used an off-the-shelf Maximum Entropy classifier (NLTK defaults), a feature set mixing structural, lexical TF-IDF word-pair, position/hierarchy, and semantic-similarity features, 10-fold cross-validation, and resampling to handle imbalance. Results: primary-secondary F-scores by class (P-S 79.3%, S-P 88.9%, MP 50.0%); selected discourse relation F-scores (Joint 57.1%, Elaboration 66.7%, Sequence 50.0%, Background 28.6%, Cause-Result 40.0%). The paper argues these results support the schema and resource. Key methodological weaknesses affect reproducibility and robustness: missing public release statement for MCDTB, incomplete reporting of inter-annotator agreement numbers and annotation guidelines, limited description of preprocessing, resampling details, hyperparameter tuning, and no uncertainty estimates for classifier metrics. Several core assumptions (paragraphs as macro leaf nodes, consistency of primary-secondary at both levels, category set sufficiency) are plausible but insufficiently validated with analyses (e.g., sensitivity to paragraph segmentation, cross-genre generality).

Observation O1: Corpus statistics (Table 6) show strong association between relation type and primary-secondary label (e.g., Joint→MP, Elaboration→P-S).
Experiment E1: Train Maximum Entropy classifiers with listed features, 10-fold CV, resampling minority class to 10x; report F-scores for primary-secondary and discourse-type recognition.
Inference I1: Reasonable classification performance indicates the schema/resource are useful for discourse-structure analysis.
Conclusion: Macro-micro unified representation plus MCDTB is appropriate for Chinese news discourse analysis and supports supervised relation and nucleus recognition tasks.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: Authors argue that existing discourse theories treat micro-level rhetorical (logical) relations and macro-level schematic (pragmatic) functions separately, which overlooks a globally-applicable primary-secondary (nuclearity) relation. They propose a macro–micro unified representation that: (a) represents discourse as a multi-layer top-down tree (title, chapter, paragraph, microstructure, EDU), (b) treats paragraphs as macro-level leaf nodes, (c) defines a primary-secondary marker (P-S, S-P, MP) applicable at both micro and macro layers, and (d) converts micro rhetorical relations (CDT/RST-style) into macro schematic pragmatic functions. To validate feasibility they annotate 97 Xinhua newswire articles (MCDTB: 533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations), measure annotator consistency on 20 docs, report descriptive statistics showing strong association between relation types and primary-secondary labels (Table 6), and run preliminary supervised classification experiments (MaxEnt, 10-fold CV, resampling) for relation and primary-secondary recognition reporting per-class F-scores. Their conclusion: the unified schema and resource are appropriate for discourse structure analysis, with caveats and plans to scale up.

P2: Primary-secondary (nuclearity) is important but usually defined only locally (micro) and not as an overall-discourse property.
Proposal: Define a unified macro–micro schema that couples micro rhetorical relations and macro schematic functions and applies a primary-secondary relation at both levels.
Design: Represent discourse as hierarchical tree (title→chapter→paragraph→microstructure→EDU), use paragraphs as macro leaf nodes, map micro rhetorical relations to macro pragmatic functions.
Annotation: Build MCDTB by annotating 97 Xinhua articles according to this schema; measure annotator consistency on sample and collect corpus statistics.
Empirical test: Train simple supervised classifiers with structural/lexical/semantic features to recognize primary-secondary and discourse relations; report performance.
Inference: Observed dependency between relation types and primary-secondary assignments and classifier performance indicate the schema/resource are useful for discourse analysis.
Conclusion: The macro–micro unified schema is a viable starting point; more data and clearer guidelines needed for broader claims.

prior_stage_inputs: Shared extraction stage: six extracted claims (C1–C6) and seven identified assumptions (A1–A7).

Paper context: MCDTB = 97 Xinhua articles; macro–micro unified schema coupling CDT/RST micro-relations with Van Dijk-inspired macro schemata; primary-secondary (P-S/S-P/MP) defined at both levels; preliminary MaxEnt experiments (nltk defaults) with resampling and 10-fold CV; corpus stats (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations).
Shared uncertainty flags: Table 4 (agreement numbers) not visible; data/code availability not stated; small size and class imbalance; limited reproducibility detail.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that discourse structure analysis benefits from a single representation that couples micro-level rhetorical relations (CDT/RST-style EDUs and rhetorical relations) with macro-level schematic/pragmatic roles (paragraph/chapter-level functions). They operationalize this by: (1) defining a hierarchical macro–micro tree (title → chapter → paragraph → microstructure → EDU) with paragraph nodes as macro leaf units; (2) introducing a primary-secondary relation (P-S, S-P, MP) that is applied at both micro and macro layers, with local/global annotation principles; (3) constructing the Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB) by annotating 97 Xinhua newswire articles (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations) on macro schematic labels, micro rhetorical labels (relying on CDT conventions), and primary-secondary arrows; (4) measuring annotator consistency over 20 documents (agreement/Kappa referenced but numeric values not shown here); and (5) running preliminary supervised experiments (Maximum Entropy classifier via nltk defaults, resampling to mitigate imbalance, 10-fold CV) using structural/lexical/semantic/positional features to predict discourse relation and primary-secondary labels. Empirical outcomes are used as evidence that (i) the schema is feasible (corpus can be built consistently enough for experiments), (ii) relation types show strong empirical association with primary-secondary assignments (Table 6 contingency counts), and (iii) baseline classifiers recover some classes with moderate F-scores (e.g., P-S/S-P reasonably high; MP and some relation types low). The paper frames the macro layer as a conversion of logical semantic relations into pragmatic schematic functions, and uses top-down + bottom-up annotation strategy to handle multi-scale composition.
logical_argument_graph: Premise: Existing discourse theories treat micro (RST/CDT) and macro (Van Dijk schematic) structures separately; nuclearity in RST is local and does not capture global discourse intention.
Inference: A unified representation that makes primary-secondary (nuclearity) explicit at both micro and macro levels can bridge logical semantics and pragmatic function.
Design decision: Represent discourse as a multi-layer tree (title→chapter→paragraph→microstructure→EDU) and use paragraphs as macro leaf nodes (A1).
Operationalization: Define P-S/S-P/MP types with local and global annotation principles (A2), and map micro rhetorical labels into macro schematic functions (A7).
Resource construction: Annotate 97 Xinhua articles (MCDTB) following the schema and a top-down + bottom-up annotation strategy (C2, C6).
Quality control: Measure annotator consistency on 20 docs (structure/relation/primary-secondary) though numeric details not visible here (C4).

Empirical test: Train MaxEnt classifiers with structural/lexical/semantic features, resample minority classes, 10-fold CV to evaluate recognition of discourse relations and primary-secondary relations (C5).
Empirical observations: Strong descriptive dependency between relation types and primary-secondary assignments (Table 6) and mixed classifier performance (Tables 8–9).
Conclusion: Unified schema is feasible and useful for discourse tasks; further scaling and formalization recommended.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a macro–micro unified discourse representation for Chinese news that attaches paragraph-level pragmatic schematic functions to standard micro-level rhetorical (CDT/RST-style) structure and defines a primary-secondary (P-S / S-P / MP) relation applicable at both scales. The authors annotated 97 Xinhua newswire articles (MCDTB: 533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations), measured annotator consistency on 20 docs (Table 4 referenced but numbers not shown), reported descriptive statistics showing strong co-occurrence patterns between relation types and primary-secondary labels (Table 6), and ran preliminary supervised experiments (NLTK Maximum Entropy, handcrafted features, 10-fold CV, resampling) to predict primary-secondary and discourse relations (per-class F-scores reported). Evidence in the manuscript supports that the schema can be operationalized and that a small resource was constructed; however, several claims are only partially supported due to missing reliability numbers, limited reproducibility detail, small corpus scale, and lack of statistical testing. I separate claims into supported, partially supported, and overstated in the identified_claims below and provide concrete strengths, concerns, comparable prior work, alternative interpretations, transparency notes, and controlled novelty assessment.
logical_argument_graph: Motivation: micro-level discourse theories (RST/CDT) capture local logical relations and nuclearity but miss pragmatic macro schematic functions → Need unified representation to capture overall discourse intention.

Representation: Define multi-layer tree (title → chapter → paragraph → microstructure → EDU), treat paragraphs as macro leaf nodes, define primary-secondary at both micro and macro levels with local/global principles.
Annotation: Apply schema to 97 Xinhua articles (MCDTB), annotate paragraph-level schematic functions, micro rhetorical relations (CDT), and primary-secondary labels.
Quality control: Annotator consistency measured on 20 docs (agreement/Kappa referenced).
Descriptive findings: Table 5 & 6 report counts; observed strong dependence between relation types and P-S/S-P/MP distributions.

Validation: Train MaxEnt classifiers with feature set (structural, lexical TF-IDF pairs, POS/word prefixes, semantic similarity to title, hierarchical/position features), resample minority classes, 10-fold CV → report F-scores for primary-secondary and selected relation types.
Conclusion: Based on construction, statistics, and preliminary classifiers, the macro–micro schema and MCDTB are appropriate and useful for discourse structure analysis.

Measurement limited to 20/97 documents and to leaf-layer only; reliability at higher macro nodes and per-category reliability remains unreported.

identified_claims.claim_text: Preliminary supervised experiments on discourse-relation recognition and primary-secondary relation recognition using features derived from the corpus yield reasonable performance (reported per-class F-scores supporting usefulness).

Table 8: primary-secondary F-scores (P-S 79.3%, S-P 88.9%, MP 50.0%). Table 9: several relation F-scores reported (Joint 57.1%, Elaboration 66.7%, etc.).
uncertainty_flags: Experimental details insufficient for replication (exact resampling procedure, random seeds, preprocessing/tokenization, feature extraction scripts, hyperparameter tuning absent).
Small sample sizes and strong class imbalance make per-class F-scores unstable; no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical tests were reported.
Choice of baseline classifier and lack of comparison to alternative models (e.g., SVM, neural models) limits interpretation of 'reasonable' performance.

Effectiveness likely depends on annotator expertise and guidelines, which are not fully described in the excerpt.

strengths.title: Clear conceptual integration of macro and micro discourse
strengths.description: The paper provides a coherent motivation and concrete design for unifying micro rhetorical relations with macro schematic/pragmatic functions and for making primary-secondary an explicit cross-level label.
evidence: Section 1 motivates the need for macro pragmatic modeling; Section 3 presents the multi-layer tree (Figures 3–7) and detailed definitions.

strengths.title: Concrete annotated resource (MCDTB) for Chinese news
strengths.description: Authors assembled and annotated a non-trivial dataset (97 Xinhua articles, 533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations) that operationalizes the proposed schema and supplies examples across categories.
evidence: Section 4.1 and Table 5 report corpus counts and describe annotations (topic, lead, paragraph topics, relations, P-S).

strengths.title: Initial empirical validation via supervised baselines
strengths.description: Preliminary classification experiments demonstrate feasibility of automatic recognition of primary-secondary labels and some relation types using straightforward features and off-the-shelf classifiers.
evidence: Section 5, Tables 7–9 report feature sets, experimental protocol (10-fold CV, MaxEnt), and per-class F-scores.

concerns.title: Missing inter-annotator agreement numbers
concerns.description: Table 4 is referenced as containing agreement and Kappa values for structure, relation, and primary-secondary labels on 20 documents, but numeric values are not shown; without these numbers the reliability of annotations cannot be judged.
evidence: Section 4.3 references Table 4 but the excerpt does not include the table or its numeric results.
Multiple reviewers in prior-stage digests flagged absence of visible agreement numbers.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include full Table 4 with per-task (structure, relation, primary-secondary) agreement and Kappa; provide per-label kappa values and confusion matrices for key categories; if agreement is low, explain adjudication and revise guidelines.

concerns.title: Dataset availability and reproducibility details absent
concerns.description: The manuscript does not state whether annotated data, annotation guidelines, or experiment code are publicly released—this hampers replication and uptake by other researchers.
evidence: No release link or repository mentioned in Sections 4 or 5; prior-stage reviewers flagged lack of explicit public release.
Experimental steps (feature extraction code, resampling scripts, random seeds) are underspecified.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a public repository or data access statement including annotation files (CoNLL/JSON/XML), full guidelines, and scripts to reproduce preprocessing, feature extraction, resampling, and training with deterministic seeds.

concerns.title: Insufficient experimental detail and robustness analysis
concerns.description: Key experimental choices (exact resampling procedure, handling of CV with resampling, tokenization, hyperparameter tuning) are not described; reported metrics lack variance estimates or statistical significance tests.

Small data and class imbalance noted in manuscript and prior-stage digests.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Describe preprocessing, exact resampling algorithm (oversample vs. replicate; performed inside training folds only?), random seeds, hyperparameter search. Report per-fold scores, standard deviations, and significance comparisons with at least one alternative classifier and a majority-class baseline.

concerns.title: Paragraph-as-leaf assumption under-validated
concerns.description: The choice to use paragraphs as macro-layer leaf nodes is pragmatic for news but may conflate multiple schematic functions within a long paragraph or split a single function across paragraphs; the paper provides little empirical validation of this segmentation choice.
evidence: Section 3.1 declares paragraphs are treated as leaf nodes and gives an example (chtb 0019), but no systematic analysis of paragraph coherence or comparisons against EDU-level macro segmentation are given.
Prior-stage reviewers flagged risk A1 about paragraph appropriateness.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct an analysis sampling paragraphs to check intra-paragraph heterogeneity (how often paragraphs contain multiple macro functions), or run a small re-annotation experiment treating EDUs as macro leaves to compare label consistency and classifier performance.

concerns.title: Potential definition-driven artifact in relation-P/S distributions
concerns.description: Observed contingency (e.g., all Elaboration labeled P-S; Joint all MP) might follow from annotation definitions or conventions rather than reflecting independent empirical regularities.
evidence: Table 6 shows deterministic patterns (Elaboration 121 P-S, Joint 151 MP). Section 3 definitions indicate some relations (joint) naturally allow multi-primary and certain subtypes (statement-illustration) are defined asymmetrically.
Authors interpret counts as strong dependence but provide no statistical control.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report conditional labeling rules from guidelines, compute statistical measures (contingency chi-squared, effect sizes), and analyze ambiguous cases where annotators disagreed to check if labels are forced by definitions.

concerns.title: Annotation guideline completeness and edge cases
concerns.description: The manuscript outlines local/global principles and category lists but lacks the full formal guideline including disambiguation rules and worked examples for difficult cases, which can drive annotator inconsistency.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes local/global principles in prose; Section 4.2 claims the annotation strategy is effective but no guideline excerpt is provided.
Aroyo & Welty (CrowdTruth) in retrieved literature stress detailed guidelines help consistency; authors do not show that level of detail.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Attach the full annotation guideline as appendix or repository file; add decision trees for common confusions and illustrative examples with adjudication rationale.

uncertainty_flags: Inter-annotator agreement numeric values (Table 4) absent in provided excerpt; annotation reliability uncertain.
Public availability of MCDTB, full annotation guidelines, and experiment code is not stated; reproducibility unresolved.
Small dataset (97 docs) and class imbalance introduce high variance in classifier metrics; reported F-scores lack confidence intervals.
Mapping rules converting micro logical relations to macro pragmatic schemata are described conceptually but formal mapping functions are not provided.
Observed dependency between relation types and P-S could be definitional or annotation-driven rather than an independent empirical phenomenon.
alternative_interpretations: The strong co-occurrence patterns in Table 6 may reflect schema definitions and annotator instructions (e.g., 'Elaboration' operationalized as nucleus in former) rather than uncovering novel linguistic regularities.

High per-class F-scores for P-S and S-P might be driven by position/hierarchical features (e.g., paragraph position correlates with topic) rather than the schema capturing deep discourse semantics; models may exploit surface cues.
Annotation and classifier performance could be genre- and corpus-specific (Xinhua news), limiting transfer to other news sources or genres with different paragraphing and schematic conventions.

Resampling to replicate minority class examples 10x could inflate apparent recall for that class on folds where duplicates appear, producing optimistic F-scores if not performed strictly inside training folds.
transparency_notes: Provide Table 4 (agreement/Kappa) and full annotation guideline as supplementary material or repository link to enable evaluation of annotation reliability.
State dataset release policy and include annotation files (with formats) plus code for preprocessing, feature extraction, and modeling with fixed random seeds.
Clarify resampling procedure (whether performed within cross-validation training folds only) and provide per-fold scores and standard deviations.
If mapping rules convert micro relations to macro schemata, include the formal mapping table or algorithm and examples showing ambiguous cases and how they were resolved.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although few prior resources tightly couple macro pragmatic schemata with micro rhetorical CDT/RST representations for Chinese news, novelty alone doesn't guarantee annotation reliability or generalizability; empirical validation (agreement, robustness, release) is required to convert novelty into community value.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the full annotation guidelines and mapping rules are released and show consistently high inter-annotator agreement across layers, then the schema would be a valuable, reproducible resource.

If experiments are rerun with robust resampling inside training folds, multiple classifiers, per-fold variance reported, and results remain stable, then the schema supports learnable cross-level signals.
If downstream tasks (e.g., summarization, MT quality estimation) empirically improve using macro-level annotations, the innovation’s practical value will be substantiated.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Extends existing Chinese micro-discourse resources (CDT) by adding a macro schematic layer and cross-level primary-secondary labels—an extension rather than a foundational theoretical shift. The operationalization for Chinese news and the MCDTB dataset are useful incremental contributions.
evidence: Manuscript builds on CDT (Li et al., 2014) and Van Dijk's macrostructure, combining them into MCDTB.
uncertainty_flags: Utility contingent on release and annotation reliability; without that, novelty is limited to conceptual framing.

novelty_lenses.rationale: If validated and widely adopted, a unified macro–micro schema that operationalizes pragmatic functions and cross-level nuclearity could change how discourse corpora are constructed and applied (e.g., enabling global-intent-aware models). However, current evidence is preliminary and scale-limited.
evidence: Conceptual design is coherent and could enable new tasks; authors claim joint annotation and give a working dataset.
uncertainty_flags: Lack of public release, missing agreement stats, and small scale make disruptive potential speculative pending stronger empirical validation.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects uncertainty about how strongly the manuscript supports its broader claims: evidence firmly supports that the authors implemented a schema and annotated a 97-document resource (high confidence), but lower confidence remains regarding annotation reliability, generalizability, reproducibility, and whether observed patterns are empirical regularities versus definitional artifacts—hence a broad interval. The lower bound accounts for missing agreement numbers and release; the upper bound assumes authors can supply missing materials and clarifications upon revision.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a coherent conceptual integration of macro (schematic/pragmatic) and micro (rhetorical/logical EDU-level) discourse representations and operationalizes a primary-secondary (P-S / S-P / MP) relation across layers.

The authors constructed a working Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB) of 97 Xinhua news articles (reported: 533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations) and produced illustrative annotated examples showing cross-level annotations.

Preliminary supervised experiments (Maximum Entropy, handcrafted features, 10-fold CV, resampling) were run to predict primary-secondary and discourse-relation labels and report per-class precision/recall/F1 numbers, demonstrating that some signal is learnable from the corpus.

Multiple reviewers flagged major reproducibility and reporting gaps: the manuscript does not (in the provided excerpt) include numeric inter-annotator agreement (Table 4 values), public-release information for the dataset/guidelines/code, or full experimental details (preprocessing, resampling specifics, seeds, hyperparameters).

The descriptive corpus statistics (Table 6) show strong co-occurrence patterns between relation types and primary-secondary labels (e.g., Joint→MP; Elaboration→P-S) — reviewers agree these counts are notable but require statistical testing and interrogation of annotation conventions before being interpreted as empirical regularities.
disagreements: Degree-of-novelty interpretation: some reviewers emphasize the contribution as a meaningful, somewhat novel extension of Chinese discourse resources (macro+micro coupling is unusual in existing corpora), while others treat the work as an incremental resource extension that needs stronger validation to be impactful. This is a controlled difference in emphasis (novelty vs. incremental).

Sufficiency of current evidence to support the claim that the schema is 'appropriate': some reviewers consider the small-scale, well-described pilot as adequate preliminary support (if qualified), whereas others view the evidence as too limited (missing IAA numbers, possible definitional artifacts, single-genre scope) to treat the schema as broadly appropriate without further validation.

Interpretation of the observed relation↔primary-secondary dependency: one view treats the contingency counts as an empirical discovery worth exploring further; the other view warns these patterns may be tautological or artifactually induced by annotation instructions (i.e., definitional coupling) unless independent validation is provided.
uncertainty_hotspots: Inter-annotator agreement (IAA) metrics: Table 4 is referenced but numeric agreement/Kappa values are absent in the excerpt; uncertainty about label reliability (especially for macro labels and cross-layer P-S judgments) is central.
Public availability of resources: it is unclear whether the MCDTB, full annotation guidelines, and experiment code are/will be released — this blocks reproducibility and independent validation.

Paragraph-as-leaf design choice: validity of treating paragraphs as atomic macro leaf nodes is untested across the corpus; intra-paragraph heterogeneity and its effect on annotations and models are uncertain.

Relation↔primary-secondary dependency causality: whether the observed deterministic-like mappings (e.g., Joint→MP, Elaboration→P-S) reflect linguistic tendencies or annotation/design choices is unresolved without statistical tests and guideline transparency.

Experimental robustness: resampling strategy, whether oversampling was applied within folds only, preprocessing/tokenization choices (Chinese segmentation, POS), classifier hyperparameters and seeds, and per-fold variation are unspecified, making reported F-scores fragile.
model_diversity_effects: Role diversity among reviewers produced complementary perspectives: structure analysts emphasized logical coherence and mapping between levels; methodology auditors highlighted reproducibility and statistical validity gaps; novelty assessors flagged potential innovation while tempering claims by methodological limitations; claim verifiers insisted on evidence-first scrutiny. This ensemble surfaces both potential innovation (macro–micro coupling) and operational weaknesses (missing IAA, missing release, underspecified experiments).

Diverse reviewer foci reduced the risk of a single blind-spot: where one reviewer accepted preliminary baselines as adequate, another flagged resampling-induced bias; where one saw novelty, another requested formal mapping rules. The result is a richer, more actionable list of missing evidence and possible artifacts than any single reviewer would deliver.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Center any next-stage decision on verification of key transparency and reliability items before treating the contribution as validated. Requested materials and analyses from authors should include: (1) the full IAA statistics (Table 4) with percent agreement, Cohen's kappa per annotation dimension and per label, confusion matrices, and description of adjudication; (2) an explicit data release statement or embargo timeline and access mechanism for MCDTB, plus the full annotation guidelines (including micro→macro mapping rules, decision trees, and edge-case examples) and annotation files in a standard, documented format; (3) complete experimental replication artifacts: preprocessing pipeline (segmentation, tokenization, POS tagger versions), feature extraction code, resampling procedure (exact algorithm, whether performed inside training folds), random seeds, classifier hyperparameters and software versions, and per-fold results with standard deviations; (4) statistical analyses quantifying the relation↔primary-secondary dependence (contingency tables, chi-squared or Fisher exact tests, effect sizes such as Cramér's V), and an audit of whether annotation rules forced some mappings (e.g., show whether primary-secondary was annotated independently of relation labels); (5) a targeted analysis of the paragraph-as-leaf assumption (sample inspection, intra-paragraph label heterogeneity rates, or a small re-segmentation experiment at EDU-level) and learning-curve or sample-scaling analysis to assess how performance changes with more data; and (6) additional robustness checks for experiments (alternative classifiers, ablation studies, sensitivity to resampling). Use the provided results of these verifications to adjudicate the strength of claims about general appropriateness vs. a promising pilot dataset. Keep the authors’ claims framed to match the level of empirical support established after these checks.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address reviewer concerns, provide the following concrete deliverables and analyses: (A) Release artifacts: deposit MCDTB annotation files, the full annotation guidelines (including explicit micro→macro mapping tables and examples of edge cases), and experiment code (preprocessing, feature extraction, modeling) in a public repository or provide clear access instructions and licenses. (B) Annotation reliability: publish Table 4 with numeric percent agreements and kappa values per layer and per label; add confusion matrices and a short qualitative analysis of common disagreements and how they were adjudicated. (C) Dependency analysis: compute and report formal statistical tests (chi-squared/Fisher exact) and effect sizes for relation vs. primary-secondary associations; explain whether some mappings follow from definitions. (D) Paragraph-as-leaf validation: analyze within-paragraph heterogeneity (how often micro EDUs suggest multiple macro functions), and if feasible run a small re-annotation experiment treating EDUs as macro leaves to compare consistency and model impact. (E) Experimental reproducibility and robustness: provide preprocessing details (Chinese segmentation and POS tools and versions), exact resampling method and confirmation resampling was done only inside training folds, random seeds, per-fold metrics and standard deviations, and include baseline comparisons (simple majority classifier), ablations (feature importances), and at least one alternative classifier (e.g., tuned logistic regression, SVM or simple neural baseline). (F) Reframe claims: temper generalization claims to match the data scale (call results 'preliminary' or 'pilot' where appropriate) and explicitly discuss limitations and plans for scaling. Implementing these steps will materially reduce the main uncertainties flagged by reviewers and enable the community to reuse and validate the resource.
transparency_report: Missing or not visible in the provided manuscript excerpt: numeric inter-annotator agreement (Table 4 values) by annotation dimension and per-label confusion matrices.

Experimental pipeline details are incomplete: Chinese segmentation/tokenization tool and version, POS tagger and model, TF-IDF vocabulary and parameters, exact resampling algorithm (oversampling replication vs. synthetic sampling), whether resampling occurred inside CV folds, random seeds, and classifier hyperparameters/software versions are not documented.
Mapping rules from micro rhetorical labels to macro schematic labels are described conceptually but lack a formal mapping table or exhaustive guideline with edge-case resolution examples.

Statistical support for descriptive claims (e.g., relation↔primary-secondary 'strong dependence') is absent: no contingency tests, effect sizes, or confidence intervals are reported for corpus statistics or classifier performance.
Per-fold experimental variability and significance testing (standard deviations, confidence intervals, or bootstrapped intervals) for classifier metrics are missing.
epistemic_limits: Synthesis is constrained by absence of access to (1) the numeric inter-annotator agreement values and confusion matrices (Table 4), (2) the annotated corpus files and full guidelines, and (3) experiment code and preprocessing details. Without those materials we cannot independently verify annotation reliability, reproduce experiments, or determine whether observed statistical patterns (e.g., Joint→MP) are empirical or definitional artifacts. The dataset is small (97 documents), so generalization beyond this pilot sample is uncertain; reported classifier metrics are sensitive to resampling and class imbalance and lack uncertainty estimates. Any interpretation of schema suitability or empirical dependencies should therefore be provisional: the manuscript demonstrates a feasible pilot implementation, but its claims about broader appropriateness and robust empirical patterns require the transparency and statistical verifications requested above.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The paper proposes a unified macro–micro discourse representation for Chinese news that couples micro-level rhetorical/EDU relations (building on CDT/RST) with macro-level schematic/pragmatic paragraph/chapter labels and a primary-secondary (P-S / S-P / MP) relation applied at both levels. The authors annotate a Macro Chinese Discourse Treebank (MCDTB) of 97 Xinhua articles (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations), report descriptive corpus statistics (including a strong co-occurrence between relation types and primary-secondary patterns), measure annotator consistency on a 20-document subset (Table 4 referenced), and run preliminary supervised baselines (NLTK Maximum Entropy, handcrafted features, 10-fold CV, resampling) for nucleus detection and relation recognition with per-class precision/recall/F1. The work reads as a pilot resource and operationalization of a macro–micro schema; however, key transparency and validation elements (numeric IAA, full guidelines, data/code release, detailed experimental protocol, and statistical tests) are missing or under-documented in the provided manuscript excerpt.
strengths: Clear conceptual motivation and coherent representation: explicit effort to link micro rhetorical relations with macro schematic/pragmatic functions and to operationalize primary-secondary across layers.
Concrete annotated resource: MCDTB (97 Xinhua articles) with cross-level examples and descriptive statistics demonstrating feasibility of annotation.

Initial empirical validation: supervised baselines and feature descriptions show that primary-secondary and some relation signals are learnable from the annotated data, providing a useful pilot benchmark.
limitations: Inter-annotator agreement reporting incomplete: Table 4 is referenced but numeric percent-agreement and Cohen's kappa values (per layer and per label), confusion matrices, and adjudication procedures are not provided in the excerpt, leaving annotation reliability uncertain.

Reproducibility gaps for data and experiments: no explicit data/code availability statement or repository link is provided; experimental details are underspecified (Chinese segmentation/POS tools and versions, exact resampling method and whether performed within folds, random seeds, per-fold results, hyperparameters), limiting replication and robustness assessment.

Small, single-genre corpus and class imbalance: 97 documents (533 paragraphs, 438 macro relations) with heavy skew to a few relation types constrains statistical power and generalizability; reported classifier metrics lack confidence intervals or variance estimates.

Unclear mapping and potential definitional circularity: formal mapping rules from micro rhetorical relations to macro schematic labels are not fully documented; the pronounced relation↔primary-secondary co-occurrence (e.g., Joint→MP, Elaboration→P-S) may reflect annotation definitions or conventions rather than independently discovered linguistic regularities absent statistical tests.
open_questions: Please provide Table 4 (numeric inter-annotator agreement): percent agreement and Cohen's kappa per annotation task (EDU/leaf structure, macro labels, relation labels, primary-secondary), plus per-label confusion matrices and a short summary of adjudication steps.

Will the MCDTB, the full annotation guidelines (including micro→macro mapping rules and edge-case decision rules), and the experiment code (preprocessing, feature extraction, resampling scripts, model training with fixed seeds) be publicly released? If delayed, provide an access policy or embargo timeline.

Was resampling performed inside each training fold only (to avoid leakage)? Specify the exact resampling algorithm (replication, SMOTE, or other), resulting class counts after resampling, and random seeds used.

Have the authors run statistical tests to quantify the relation↔primary-secondary dependency (e.g., contingency chi-squared or Fisher exact tests and effect sizes like Cramér's V)? If not, please run and report them and clarify whether annotation rules could have forced any deterministic mappings.

To justify paragraphs as macro leaf nodes: how often did annotators observe intra-paragraph heterogeneity (multiple macro schematic functions within one paragraph)? Provide sampling statistics or a short re-segmentation analysis (EDU-level macro leaves) to show sensitivity to this choice.

Provide per-fold classifier metrics or bootstrapped confidence intervals and at least one alternative classifier and basic ablation (feature importance) to demonstrate robustness of the reported baselines.
consensus_snapshot: Reviewers agree the paper presents a coherent and reasonably motivated macro–micro discourse representation and that building MCDTB is a meaningful pilot contribution for Chinese news discourse.

There is consistent recognition that preliminary supervised experiments show learnable signal for primary-secondary and some relation classes, but that experimental reporting is underspecified and results are fragile due to small data and class imbalance.
All reviewers request fuller transparency: numeric IAA, full annotation guidelines and mapping rules, public data/code release, and rigorous experimental detail (resampling, seeds, per-fold metrics).

Interpretation of the relation↔primary-secondary contingency: some see the counts as an interesting empirical pattern to explore further; others caution these patterns may be tautological or enforced by annotation definitions and thus require statistical and procedural disentangling.
uncertainty_snapshot: Main epistemic uncertainty centers on annotation reliability (missing numeric IAA), data/code availability, and whether observed statistical patterns are empirical or artefactual.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper presents a coherent proposal and a concrete pilot resource (MCDTB) that couples macro schematic functions with micro rhetorical trees and a cross-layer primary-secondary annotation. The annotation and example trees make the schema tangible, and preliminary classifiers show learnable signal for nucleus detection and some relation classes.

Strengths: Clear conceptual integration; a working annotated corpus with illustrative examples; initial supervised baselines that demonstrate feasibility.

Limitations: Numeric inter-annotator agreement is not provided in the excerpt (Table 4 missing), obstructing judgment of annotation reliability; data/code/guideline availability and experimental protocol details (preprocessing, resampling, seeds, hyperparameters, per-fold results) are absent, hindering reproducibility; corpus scale (97 single-source articles) and class imbalance limit generalizability; mapping rules from micro relations to macro schemata are not formalized, raising the possibility that observed relation↔P-S co-occurrence reflects definitional conventions rather than independent empirical patterns.

Open Questions: See explicit list above requesting (1) Table 4 numeric IAA, (2) data/guideline/code release policy and links, (3) resampling implementation and seeds, (4) statistical tests for relation↔P-S dependence, (5) paragraph-as-leaf validation, and (6) per-fold/CI reporting and alternative baselines.

Transparency: Missing items are enumerated — IAA details, full guidelines including mapping and edge cases, annotation files, and full experimental artifacts (preprocessing, resampling, seeds). Without these, core claims about reliability and generality must remain provisional.

Overall conclusion (analytical synthesis): The manuscript documents a promising pilot resource and an operational macro–micro schema for Chinese news discourse. To move from a pilot demonstration to a robust community resource and to substantiate broader claims about schema appropriateness and empirical regularities, the authors should supply the requested transparency items, statistical analyses, and robustness checks. After these verifications the community can better judge novelty and practical utility.

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound reflects uncertainty introduced by missing reproducibility materials (IAA numbers, guidelines, data/code) and small single-genre dataset; upper bound reflects that the manuscript credibly reports a working pilot resource, concrete annotations, and baseline experiments that plausibly support preliminary claims. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review.
